In other words, this “scepticism” is really nothing other than empiricism.
Empiricism holds that there can be no truth unless discourse is related to reality.
Simply because discourse itself, having no content of its own, would be impossible without reality.

Before rationalism gives way completely and transforms itself into empiricism, however, it makes one final attempt to save its “immanent” conception of truth: the idea that truth is a discourse produced by reason alone that fully satisfies reason.
Naive rationalism had ended in the first scepticism because it regarded all coherent discourses as true even though they contradicted one another.
Critical rationalism had ended in the second “scepticism”—that is, in empiricism—because the only way it could avoid contradictions was by identifying different discursive contents.

The third and final form of rationalism, which I would call reflective rationalism—rationalism that turns thought back upon itself—tries to find a middle path between naive and critical rationalism by introducing the concept of self-evidence.
This form of rationalism admits that reason produces discourses that are mutually incompatible and that we do not always have any way of choosing which should be called true and which false.
Where possible, it must still use the method of identification.
Where identification is no longer possible, it must suspend judgement sceptically. It must refrain from choosing and admit that, in the case at hand, there is no knowledge or valid idea available.
But reason can also produce another kind of discourse: a discourse that is self-evident.
Such a discourse, reflective rationalism claims, can be confidently declared true without stepping outside its own boundaries and without appealing to any extra-rational reality.
Any discourse contradicting such a self-evident proposition must therefore be false.
Examples of these supposed self-evident truths include statements such as:
“a part is smaller than the whole,”
“a straight line is the shortest distance between two points.”
To say the opposite—or simply something different—such as “a part is equal to the whole,” would therefore amount to saying something false.
This form of rationalism proved the most persistent of all.
It appears in almost every philosopher. Even after Hegel demonstrated its inconsistency, it continued to be defended by later bourgeois followers of pre-Hegelian philosophy.
Yet from the beginning it faced an objection that has never disappeared and never can disappear, because reflective rationalism has never been able to prove its own truth.
There is no doubt that supposedly “self-evident” truths are just as relative as the supposed convincingness of myths.
What is self-evident to one person may not be self-evident at all to another. The second person may even regard it as false.
History has also shown that most alleged “self-evident truths” are either false or completely arbitrary assumptions.
I have already used the example that, in the infinite, a part can be equal to the whole. Endless examples of this kind could be given.
The decisive blow against the theory of “self-evidence” came in the nineteenth century with the discovery of non-Euclidean geometries.
For centuries, the geometrical axioms associated with Euclid had been regarded as the model of self-evident, a priori truth.
It turned out that they were not truths at all, but arbitrary propositions that could be altered.
A straight line, for example, need not be the shortest path between two points.
And if we try to apply these axioms to real space, it turns out that, one way or another, we simply do not know whether they are true or false.
The inconsistency of reflective rationalism—and therefore of rationalism in general—is consequently no longer in doubt.

So if philosophy knows that its knowledge is partial but still wants to claim that this knowledge is true without falling into scepticism—and if it gives up this claim, philosophy simply loses its meaning—then it must reject rationalism.

It must accept that truth—that is, convincing discourse—is nothing other than the correspondence between discourse, which is articulated, communicable, and coherent, and a reality that exists independently of the discourse expressing it.
In other words, philosophy must accept the fundamental thesis of empiricism.
But only genuine Hegelian-Marxist empiricism can save philosophy from dying in scepticism.
I would prefer to call this genuine form of empiricism experimentalism or technicism.
Traditional, pre-Hegelian empiricism is just as inconsistent as traditional rationalism.
We must therefore now examine what this traditional and inconsistent empiricism consists in.
From the rationalist point of view, “truth” is a quality belonging to discourse itself—to reason, or logos. It can therefore be discovered by purely discursive, rational, or logical means.
Discourse in itself has no content at all. It can therefore be neither true nor false.
Its content enters it from outside. In other words, content comes from a “reality” that exists independently of discourse.

It produces words and combinations of words whose meanings are inseparably tied to a completely determinate reality. Anyone who understands the meaning of the discourse therefore knows which reality it refers to.
If the semantic content of a given discourse corresponds to a real content—to the very reality designated by the discourse—then the discourse is true.
If it does not, it is false.
It should also be noted that empiricism was originally just as “naive” and credulous as rationalism.
Until something convinced people otherwise, they were naturally inclined to regard every discourse about reality as true.

That is, human beings assumed that whenever they spoke about some reality, the semantic structure of their discourse automatically reproduced the real structure of that reality itself, provided only that the discourse was articulated, meaningful, and coherent.
There is therefore almost no difference between naive empiricism and naive rationalism.
Both assume that every coherent discourse is convincing and therefore true.
The only difference is in the reason they give.
Naive rationalism regards a discourse as convincing simply and solely because it is coherent.
Naive empiricism calls every coherent discourse true because it assumes that every coherent discourse automatically corresponds to the reality it claims to describe.
The difference between rationalism and empiricism becomes important only when empiricism ceases to be naive.
And it stopped being naive for much the same reason that rationalism had been forced to abandon its own naivety.
Rationalism had discovered that human beings could produce mutually incompatible discourses.
Empiricism likewise had to recognize that several discourses about one and the same reality could be mutually incompatible, which means they could not all equally be regarded as true.
Different people can speak differently about the same reality.
Indeed, the same person may say different things about the very same reality at different moments in their life.
This fact produces a form of empirical scepticism.
It claims that reality is “hidden” from discourse, that its content cannot be transmitted in words, and therefore that no discourse can really be true.
To avoid this scepticism, empiricism becomes “critical” and adopts a method similar to the one used by critical rationalism when it tried to escape rationalist scepticism.
First, critical empiricism introduces an intermediary between reality and discourse—that is, between reality and reason.
Reality does not itself give human beings the immediate ability to speak about it. Human discourse therefore does not relate directly to reality itself.
Reality “reveals” itself immediately not to discourse, but to what we call sensory experience: what is seen, heard, and so on.
When human beings speak about reality, then, they do not refer immediately to reality itself. They refer to its “image” as contained in sensory experience.
The semantic content of discourse always and automatically corresponds to the sensory content of experience. In that sense, every coherent discourse can be regarded as “true.”
Its sensory content therefore does not always correspond to real content.
When I am ill, for example, honey may taste bitter to me even though “in reality” it is sweet, and so on.
Since we call true only a discourse whose semantic content corresponds to a real content—the reality it denotes—we cannot regard every discourse as convincing or true.
True discourse is possible, but false discourse is equally possible.
This explains why human beings can produce many incompatible discourses about reality.
As an “empirico-critical” explanation of the undeniable fact that incompatible discourses can concern one and the same reality, this is convincing enough.
The difficulty begins as soon as we raise the problem of the criterion of truth:
How do we distinguish true discourses from false ones?
The solution proposed by critical empiricism was already clearly formulated by Democritus, and in principle it has remained unchanged ever since.
It consists in distinguishing between so-called primary and secondary qualities.
Primary qualities are those features of sensory experience that have corresponding qualities in reality itself.
Secondary qualities, by contrast, do not exist in reality at all. They belong only to sensory experience, though of course they still arise through our encounter with reality.
In our example, honey merely seems sweet or bitter. “In reality,” it is neither.
Discourses whose semantic content corresponds to secondary qualities are therefore, strictly speaking, neither true nor false.
There is no way to choose between them. Each is “true” for the person—and only for the person—who states it.
If a sick person says that honey tastes bitter, they are just as right as a perfectly healthy person who says that it tastes sweet.
There is no point arguing about tastes and colours.
Secondary qualities are simply personal or subjective “tastes” to which nothing objectively corresponds “in reality.”
Empirical scepticism is therefore right when discourse concerns secondary qualities.
But it is wrong to overlook the existence of primary qualities, which belong both to sensory experience and to reality itself and are therefore reflected in discourse.
If the semantic structure of a discourse corresponds to the primary qualitative structure of reality, then the discourse is true in every sense—“objectively” true.
